generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, evaluation is where you weigh one judgement against another. A single source rarely settles a question: rival readings compete to account for the same evidence. To evaluate is to ask which fits the evidence better, and why, how large and representative the sample was, whether the finding has held up elsewhere, whether a simpler account would do. Across the school this looks different by subject, a coach weighing two session designs, a scientist weighing two readings of a test, but the verdict always comes with reasons drawn from the evidence, not from preference.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport coaching students write about the same training session plan.

Tom takes the plan apart neatly: here is the aim, here is the drill chosen for it, here is the reasoning. The account is accurate, and it stops there. Tom has analysed the plan but not weighed it: there is no sense of how strong it is, or how it stands against any other way of coaching the same aim. This is analysis without evaluation.

Amara goes further. Having seen the parts, she sets this plan against a rival design and asks which better serves the aim, given the players and the evidence on skill learning. The first packs in more repetitions but blocks them by drill; the second spaces and mixes them, which research on retention favours. Amara judges the second stronger on balance, and says why. This is evaluation.

Both students understood the plan. Only Amara weighed its relative value against an alternative, with reasons.
generatedProse.summary: In the School of Sport, evaluation means weighing the relative value of a judgement against alternatives, with reasons drawn from the evidence, rather than judging it in isolation. You can now tell evaluation apart from analysis and choose an evaluative question to ask of a session plan or a study. The next lesson completes the set: synthesis draws several evaluated sources together into an argument of your own.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Amara do that Tom did not?

items.text: She weighed the session plan against a rival design and judged which better served the aim, with reasons.
She separated the plan into its aim, drill and reasoning.
She summarised the plan more accurately.
She described the drills in more detail.

feedback.correct: That's right. Weighing the plan against a rival design, with reasons, is evaluation.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Tom already took the plan apart. Look for what Amara ADDED.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara evaluated: weighing the session plan against an alternative and judging which better served the aim, with reasons. Both had already analysed it.
